title: Conversation stream ops demo — Redwood hosted chat walkthrough
summary: Redwood AE + SE ran a hosted chat generation walkthrough focused on streaming behavior, parameter tuning, and resilience patterns for a healthcare customer. Key topics: partial response streaming, tokenization and cost tradeoffs, retry/backoff strategies, KV cache hints, and secure private deployment considerations for PHI-adjacent usage. Agreed next steps include security docs, a sandbox invite, and a small latency benchmark run with a sample prompt set.
topics: console quick tour and Optimize suggestions

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-14 16:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Sara Kim (Redwood AE), Noah Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (Veridian Head of AI), Daniel Brooks (Platform Eng), Priya Nair (InfoSec)

[00:00] Sara Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Im Sara, AE on the account, and with me is Noah, our SE. Really appreciate you taking the time, Maya, Priya, Daniel. Quick plan — 30-ish minute hosted chat demo, then 10–15 minutes for ops/security Q&A and next steps. Sound good?

[00:18] Maya Lopez: Yep that works. Were primarily curious about streaming behavior and how retries impact user UX. We're in healthcare so also security is big for us, Priya will chime in.

[00:27] Noah Chen: Great. Ill share my screen and kick off a quick sandbox run. Note: I'll run against our hosted API endpoint — same surface you'd see in production. Ill show streaming partials, param effects, and a basic retry pattern.

[00:42] [screen share starts / typing sounds]

[00:50] Noah Chen: Ok pasted a prompt that simulates a patient triage chat — short context, then we stream. Youll see tokens arrive incrementally. The client gets delta events; client can render partials while we continue generation.

[01:12] Maya Lopez: Are we getting full sentences or token fragments? Were worried about mid-sentence updates showing to end-users.

[01:20] Noah Chen: Good question. Streaming pushes partial deltas — usually word pieces depending on tokenizer. You can configure the client to buffer until punctuation or until a threshold of characters before flush. Redwood's SDK includes utilities for "finalize-on" heuristics. In practice teams either show live typing or show a small spinner until sentence complete.

[01:42] Daniel Brooks: How does this affect latency metrics? If we buffer, does that add to perceived latency?

[01:50] Noah Chen: Yes, buffering trades off perceived latency vs jittery UI. We instrument tokenArrival timestamps in the Console and in the per-request logs, so you can see median token time, 95th, etc. If you buffer to sentence boundary, perceived latency could add a few hundred ms depending on generation speed.

[02:12] Priya Nair: On security — we need to know about data retention and key management. Patient data is involved; do you offer KMS/HSM integrations and can we run in a private VPC?

[02:24] Sara Kim: Short answer: yes. For enterprise customers we support KMS integrations and Redwood Private with a VPC option or on-prem package. We also provide audit logs and token-level tracing. I will send the SOC two summary and compliance pack after the call.

[02:40] Maya Lopez: Thanks. Also curious about cost — streaming obviously increases token counts due to intermediate tokens?

[02:49] Noah Chen: Streaming itself doesn't change tokenization cost — you pay for generated tokens. But parameters like max_tokens, temperature, and prompt length drive cost. Also prefix caching (we call it KV cache) can save tokens for repeated contexts. Note some transcripts show KV cash in ASR, ha, we get that a lot.

[03:10] [demo continues — switching to parameter playground]

[03:18] Noah Chen: Heres a quick alter of temperature from 0.0 to 0.8 so you can see variability. Lower temperature = deterministic answers (good for structured clinical flows). Higher temperature = more creative. Also well demo max_tokens and stopping sequences to avoid run-on outputs.

[03:40] Maya Lopez: For our use case we want deterministic, short answers for triage. So temperature 0.0 and a constrained max_tokens sounds right. Any risk of truncation mid-sentence?

[03:50] Noah Chen: If you set max_tokens too low then yes. You can check Console latency and token usage; Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization/params for cost. For short clinical responses, teams often set max_tokens 40-80 and define stop tokens.

[04:10] Daniel Brooks: Can you show retry behavior? We see intermittent 503s in other providers and want to understand best practices.

[04:18] Noah Chen: Absolutely — Ill simulate a transient failure. Best pattern: client-side idempotency key + exponential backoff with jitter. For chat we recommend resuming with the conversation history and the same idempotency key to avoid duplicate user-visible replies. If streaming was partially delivered, you can either stitch partial and re-request the remainder or mandate full restart.

[04:44] [simulated network error / retry log appears]

[04:50] Noah Chen: See here — initial request failed at token 7, client retried with same idempotency key, server recognized partial KV cache and resumed generation from cached attention state where possible. Note: not all model variants preserve full streaming-resume semantics; fallback is to regenerate from history.

[05:12] Maya Lopez: That resume behavior sounds ideal but also complicated. How deterministic is that across model versions and quantizations?

[05:20] Noah Chen: Good point. Resume and precise token-level resume is model-variant dependent. Our runtime will attempt a compatible fallback model and we expose the model-version in the response. If a resume isn't possible, we signal that and the client can either present the partial and then the regenerated full response or retry with a fresh request. You can configure fallback policies in the Console for automatic model variant selection.

[05:46] Priya Nair: For PHI, does Redwood redact logs or can we disable logging entirely?

[05:53] Sara Kim: We have options — redact PII/PHI at the ingestion point, and for Private deployments you can opt out of retention or keep logs only in your VPC. Ill include the log-retention matrix in the docs we send.

[06:08] [Noah opens Console - showing per-route dashboards]

[06:16] Noah Chen: Quick Console tour: per-route latency percentiles, token-level cost breakdown, and Optimize suggestions. Optimize will suggest batching sizes and quantization choices given your request distribution. For example, if most requests are short (<64 tokens) we suggest smaller batch thresholds to reduce latency.

[06:36] Daniel Brooks: Does batching hurt 95th percentile latency for sporadic single requests?

[06:42] Noah Chen: It can if you wait for a batch to fill. We do continuous batching with a max-wait threshold so single requests are served without large delays. You can tune batching policies per-route.

[06:58] Maya Lopez: Any simple code snippet for retries + streaming reassembly?

[07:04] Noah Chen: Yep, Ill paste a snippet in the follow-up but in JS its basically: open stream, accumulate partial chunks, persist an idempotency key and last-confirmed token index, on failure retry with same key and request conversation history and last-confirmed index. If server can resume, it returns a resume token marker, otherwise you get a regeneration marker.

[07:28] [minor crosstalk — someone types a question in chat]

[07:35] Maya Lopez: Regarding model selection — we prefer open models for cost reasons. How does Redwood surface model perf profiles?

[07:43] Sara Kim: We have a model catalog with benchmarks (latency and cost per token) for each model variant and recommended quantization profiles. The Console shows verified profiles and runbooks for edge cases. We'll share a model profile spreadsheet as well.

[07:58] Maya Lopez: And about regional failover — we need EU residency for some data. Is there auto-failover without cross-border copying?

[08:08] Sara Kim: You can pin a region per-deployment. For Hosted API, you can prefer region routing; for strict data residency we recommend Redwood Private deployed in your EU region. We also support routing policies that avoid cross-border failover.

[08:26] Daniel Brooks: Curious about observability — do you expose request traces (OpenTelemetry) to our tracing backend?

[08:33] Noah Chen: Yes, you can forward traces or we can inject trace IDs in the response headers and logs. We integrate with common tracing backends.

[08:42] [Noah runs a short latency benchmark live]

[08:50] Noah Chen: Running a 100-request sample against a mid-sized open model in our hosted cluster. Median token time is ... let it run.

[09:10] Maya Lopez: While that runs — one more on retries: do you charge for token duplicates on retries?

[09:16] Sara Kim: You pay for generated tokens. If a retry regenerates tokens, those tokens are billable. For heavy retry situations we suggest routes with more robust SLOs or reserved capacity to reduce transient errors. Dedicated pools also reduce noisy-neighbor failures that cause retries.

[09:40] [benchmark completes — numbers posted]

[09:44] Noah Chen: Results — median latency 220ms, p95 420ms for our sample prompts. Token cost estimate shown in Console. These numbers are for the selected model and small prompt size.

[10:00] Maya Lopez: Those look promising. Wed like a small benchmark run with our prompts and our expected concurrency.

[10:07] Sara Kim: Totally. Noah will send a small benchmark harness you can run from your environment; well also provide a hosted sandbox if you prefer.

[10:18] Priya Nair: On compliance again — can we get a SOC2 report and the specific KMS integration docs?

[10:25] Sara Kim: Yes, action item — Ill send SOC2 summary and KMS/HSM integration notes.

[10:32] [wrap-up and recap]

[10:35] Sara Kim: Recap: shared notes on streaming, retry/resume patterns, buffering UX tradeoffs, Console/Optimize tour, and security options. Next steps: security pack + sandbox + benchmark harness and follow-up SE deep dive.

[10:48] Maya Lopez: Great, appreciate the time. Looking forward to the sandbox.

[10:52] Sara Kim: Thanks everyone. Well follow up with the items in the next 24–48 hours.

[END]
